# Hardware & Networking

## Data Center Watch: Token Spend Growth Accelerates in October Amid Mixed GPU
Rental and Memory Pricing

  
---  
  
By [Joseph Cardoso
AC](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14274259&ad=5055129378&h=ClBHs3Z&sig=4QvYgXOHylxs4bmcgbWTlBEx54w&v=2&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/analyst/N694339),

[Click here for the full document and
disclaimers](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14274259&ad=5055129378&h=nFaffSd&sig=5TXzP7GAVQWwoZrPZjjwOCnmdJj&v=2&isig=70q1D23Dv9XbewubqiiB5dKcYUB&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/sh0bq15j/GPS-5505036-0/87100791-c259-4dd1-9eae-c53ae11a7303)

In the Data Center Watch report, we outline key data points relevant to AI
infrastructure demand, including LLM token volumes and prices, GPU rental
prices, and memory costs. Taken together, the latest data on LLM token spend
growth suggest AI infrastructure demand remains strong, but pricing signals
from GPU rentals and memory spot prices were more mixed. LLM token spend
growth accelerated to +40% m/m in October from +28% m/m in September, driven
by strong volume growth and a rebound in volume-weighted pricing, primarily
reflecting a mix shift toward higher-priced models, particularly Claude Opus
5.5. Meanwhile, sequentially, GPU rental prices declined further for A100s,
while H100 pricing rebounded and B200 price growth accelerated. With regards
to memory, DRAM spot prices rebounded following September’s modest decline,
while NAND prices declined for a second consecutive month. Growth in contract
prices for both DRAM and NAND is expected to moderate further to +13% and +18%
q/q, respectively, in 4Q26E, versus +16% and +21% q/q in 3Q26. Key highlights
from Data Center Watch report:

  * Token spend growth accelerated sequentially on OpenRouter in October. LLM growth trends on OpenRouter in October were strong: token volume tracked to +25% m/m and 33x y/y, while average pricing tracked to -5% m/m and +9% y/y. Net-net, overall spending was robust, with growth tracking to +40% m/m and 20x y/y. Volume-weighted pricing increased +12% m/m and declined -38% y/y, with the m/m increase driven by: (1) mix shift toward higher-priced models, particularly Opus 5.5, which added ~7.9 tn tokens at a premium price; and (2) same-model repricing, with GPT-5.6 Sol pricing doubling as its 50% discount lapsed while Kimi K3 and DeepSeek v4 Pro saw increased output prices.
  * A100 GPU rental prices declined further in October, while H100 prices rebounded and B200 price growth accelerated. Sequential growth trends for GPU rental prices remained mixed in October for Nvidia GPUs with regards to non-hyperscaler capacity. A100 prices declined -3.5% m/m, while H100 prices rebounded +6.5% m/m and B200 prices increased +4.7% m/m. Pricing for B200s was 2.1x that of H100s, down sequentially, while H100 pricing was 1.9x that of A100s, up sequentially.
  * Growth in contract prices for both DRAM and NAND is expected to moderate further in 4Q26. Per TrendForce, conventional DRAM and NAND contract prices are expected to grow +10–15% q/q and +15–20% q/q in 4Q26, respectively vs. +16% q/q for DRAM and +21% q/q for NAND in 3Q26. TrendForce attributed the moderation to prior price increases, pressure on consumer demand, sufficient buyer inventories in client SSDs, and long-term pricing agreements for some server DRAM suppliers. However, AI server demand and capacity allocation toward server products continue to support pricing, with enterprise SSDs the only category expected to see price growth accelerate in 4Q26.



## LLM Token Tracker

Our LLM Token Tracker captures a single week of usage and pricing data each
month, providing a monthly snapshot or sampling of trends across ~300 LLMs
listed on OpenRouter, an aggregation platform that routes API requests to
models through a single endpoint. Keep in mind, OpenRouter skews towards
developer, startup, and agentic-coding traffic and excludes first-party API
volume (direct OpenAI/Anthropic, hyperscaler-hosted endpoints).

Key takeaways:

  * Token volume growth moderated in the month of October, following strength in September. Token volume growth moderated on a sequential basis in October, expanding +25% m/m (vs. +71% in September and +47% in August), and 33x y/y (vs. 30x in September and 28x in August). Volumes for closed-weight models (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.), which represented 28% of the total (vs. 27% in September and 33% in August), saw growth moderate in October, expanding +30% m/m (vs. +39% in September and +66% in August) and 12x y/y (vs. 10x in September and 14x in August). Volumes for open-weight models (DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, etc.) saw growth moderate more sharply in October, expanding +21% m/m (vs. +83% in September and +39% in August) and 97x y/y (vs. 101x in September and 56x in August).
  * Token VWAP rebounded in October. Volume-weighted pricing increased +12% m/m and declined -38% y/y, with the m/m increase driven by: (1) mix shift toward higher-priced models, particularly Opus 5.5, which added ~7.9 tn tokens at a premium price; and (2) same-model repricing. Volume-weighted pricing for open-weight models declined -5% m/m (vs. -11% in September and -17% in August) and rose +24% y/y (vs. +30% in September and +60% in August) vs. +14% m/m in October for closed-weight models (vs. -15% in September and -37% in August) and +37% y/y (vs. ~flat in September and -29% in August). At the same time, average token pricing decreased -5% m/m in October (vs. +4% in September and -5% in August), while year-over-year growth moderated, with pricing expanding +9% y/y (vs. +20% in September and +5% in August).
  * Token spending growth accelerated in October. Net-net, token spending growth strengthened in October, expanding +40% m/m (vs. +28% in September and +7% in August) and 20x y/y (vs. 14x in September and 12x in August). Spending for closed-weight models, which represented 77% of the total (vs. 72% in September and 78% in August), saw growth accelerate in October, increasing +49% m/m (vs. +18% in September and +4% in August) and 16x y/y (vs. 10x in September and 10x in August). By comparison, spending for open-weight models saw growth moderate sharply in October, increasing +15% m/m (vs. +64% in September and +16% in August) and 121x y/y (vs. 132x in September and 89x in August).
  * One model overlapped in the top five by spend versus usage. The top five models in October based on token usage were: (1) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, (2) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, (3) GLM 5.3 Flash, (4) Tencent’s Hy4 preview, and (5) MiMo-V2.6-Flash, accounting for 47%+ of total token volume, down from 53%+ and from 50%+ in August. However, on a spending basis, the top five models in October were: (1) Claude Opus 5.5, (2) Tencent’s Hy4 preview, (3) Claude Sonnet 5.5, (4) GPT-6 Astra, and (5) GPT-6.1 Sol, accounting for 54% of total token spend, up from 50% in September and 48% in August.

## GPU Rental Price Tracker

Key takeaways based on Bloomberg indices:

  * A100 rental prices declined further m/m in October. A100 rental prices tracked to $1.53/GPU-hour on average in October, down -3.5% m/m (vs. -3.0% m/m in September and -0.7% m/m in August).
  * H100 rental prices rebounded m/m in October; H100-to-A100 ratio moved higher. H100 rental prices tracked to $2.83/GPU-hour on average in October, up +6.5% m/m (vs. -2.0% m/m in September and +0.4% m/m in August). The H100-to-A100 price ratio tracked to 1.85x on average in October (vs. 1.67x in September and 1.65x in August).
  * B200 rental price growth accelerated m/m in October; B200-to-H100 ratio moved lower. B200 rental prices tracked to $6.00/GPU-hour on average in October, up +4.7% m/m (vs. +1.8% m/m in September and -1.5% m/m in August). The B200-to-H100 price ratio tracked to 2.12x on average in October (vs. 2.16x in September, 2.08x in August, 2.12x in July, and 2.58x around index launch in Sep-25).

## Memory Price Tracker

Key takeaways based on Bloomberg data:

  * DRAM spot prices rebounded in October, with DDR5 16Gb up more than 3x y/y. DDR5 16Gb spot prices reached $51.80 in October, increasing +4.4% m/m (vs. $49.60 in September and $50.20 in August) and +227% y/y (vs. $15.85 in October 2025), marking a return to monthly increases following September’s modest decline.
  * NAND spot prices declined further in October; NAND 1Tb remains up nearly 4x y/y. NAND 1Tb spot prices tracked to $29.40 in October, declining -2.6% m/m (vs. $30.20 in September and $30.50 in August) and increasing +298% y/y (vs. $7.38 in October 2025), marking the second consecutive monthly decline following August’s increase.
  * DRAM and NAND contract prices expanded +16% and +21% q/q in 3Q26; contract prices to expand into 4Q26E as well, albeit at a moderated pace. As per TrendForce, DRAM contract prices expanded +16% q/q in 3Q26 (vs. +56% q/q in 2Q26), while NAND contract prices increased +21% q/q (vs. +58% q/q in 2Q26). For 4Q26E, DRAM and NAND contract prices are expected to expand +13% q/q and +18% q/q, respectively.

##

  
---  
  
By [Doug Anmuth

Please see attached our J.P. Morgan US Internet Comp Sheet priced at the close
Friday, October 23, including JPM estimates and valuation multiples across the
52 companies in our Internet coverage universe. Additionally, given the strong
focus on AI capex spending and capital requirements, we’ve included our
Hyperscaler Metrics charts in Figures 3 and 4. We now project hyperscaler
capex to increase from ~$900B in 2026 to $1.6T in 2027, +77% growth. Please
feel free to contact us if you’d like either Excel file or if you have any
questions.

Upcoming catalysts this week: 1) Internet earnings including GOOGL (10/28),
EBAY (10/28), ETSY(10/28), AMZN (10/29), RDDT (10/29), PINS (10/29), & RBLX
(10/29); 2) SPCX lock up expiration on Monday,10/26, for 328M shares, which
increases the float by 8%.

What Stands Out:

  * 1 - Our market cap-weighted coverage was down -4% last week, underperforming the SPX which was ~flat, while the Internet average was up +1%. The top performing stocks were CART (+13%) & SPOT (+10%), while the biggest decliners were META (-9%) & RDDT (-8%). 
  * 2 - META shares were down -9% last week despite delivering solid [3Q results](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14273338&ad=5054350030&h=rqlwbXk&sig=D3b6zDMo9EFNt7Pg0LTG2ZYZm9A&v=2&isig=7nBwVSfJJy2jSD5PnWBEpBtVKlv&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/-dgh83cq/GPS-5500387-0/6582b0dd-9601-4959-a226-1f054ee5727a) & better than expected 4Q guidance, as investor scrutiny intensified around capex for the AI infrastructure buildout & a potential equity raise. Meta is introducing a new class of non-voting Class C shares in January 2027, and investor focus has shifted to the 14C filing details which suggest Meta has discussed an equity raise & recapitalization for at least the last several months, as well as management’s view that it may need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars over the next several years. Meta talked down the hundreds of billions figure, instead suggesting that it was more of a theoretical maximum computed to determine what level of equity financing would trigger Mark to lose voting control. Meta also stated that it is not actually a description of its current equity financing needs or plans. We believe this is true from an equity perspective as we view equity as a minority of the capital Meta will raise in coming years. But we are currently modeling ~$350B in cumulative debt raises between 2026-2030. In terms of a potential equity raise, we believe Meta could move forward before the C shares in January 2027, though Mark would have a very modest dilution of voting control. The sooner the better in our view as it would remove the overhang and the Street now knows it will have non-voting shares in Jan'27. While Meta did not provide specific insights into 2027 total expenses or capex, we raised both coming out of earnings—along w/our revenue—and now project total expenses of $217B and capex of $255B (+78%). 
  * 3 - SPCX shares were up 1% last week. 3Q earnings (see our [takeaways](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14273338&ad=5054350030&h=AW_VTok&sig=UdBstRGmOBxEqevjj125Sr3Abip&v=2&isig=JaWX9ldDs0nBK1AZz79QXiXXtPd&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/-gt5e3mv/GPS-5498515-0/6582b0dd-9601-4959-a226-1f054ee5727a)) showed strong execution across Space, Connectivity, & SI. That execution drove upside to 3Q results, the 1Q revenue guide, & the YE27 target of $500B-$1T ARR on 13GW+ of cumulative compute exiting ‘27. Key debates from our investor discussions were: 1) SI monetization, incl. the magnitude of Vera Rubin (VR) upside vs. the current $50B+/GW high end; 2) how SPCX holds infra buildout costs in the range of $30B-40B/GW despite the shift to higher priced VRs; & 3) how SPCX will fund SI investments. Given SPCX’s bigger ramp in compute in 2027—which we put at 7.3 GW to end 2027 at just over 10 GW total—we now model 2027 capex of $295B (+238%). Beyond broader AI capex & capital concerns, SPCX also faced 1.3B shares coming unlocked last Thursday (45% increase to the float)), with another 328M unlocking Monday, 10/26 (8% increase to the float). The next key catalysts are Starship Flight 15 (likely November, w/ a possible ship & booster catch) & the 798M share unlock on 12/8 (18% increase to the float).
  * 4 - CART shares were up +13% for the week, including up +9% on Friday after [reports](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14273338&ad=5054350030&h=L25nqJZ&sig=SUp2XvtAAZglWmCDHWdqc6Wh3YO&v=2&url=https://www.theinformation.com/articles/instacart-exploring-sale) indicated that it has been working with an investment bank on strategic options including a potential sale, and had held initial talks with Uber and DoorDash, although talks with Uber do not appear to be ongoing. CART shares are up 25% YTD on consecutive beat-and-raise quarters, but there have been concerns around increasing competition from 3P delivery players like DASH & UBER (especially since the Costco partnership announcement), as well as retailers like AMZN and WMT, and agentic risk. Before the above news came out, CART was trading at ~$13B market cap and we would expect a premium of at least 25%+ or $16B+ market cap.
  * 5 - EBAY shares were up +1% this week, as mgmt announced a RIF of ~9% of headcount or ~1,100 employees based on Dec’25 ending 12,300 employees. EBAY expects to incur $130M-$150M in restructuring charges, with the majority of these charges to be recognized in 4Q26. EBAY is expected to realign teams towards top strategic priorities, and high growth areas. Separately, EBAY also said that 3Q results will come in above guidance, which was expected by investors.
  * 6 - SPOT shares were up 10% and NFLX shares were down -7% last week after both companies reported 3Q earnings. [SPOT delivered solid 3Q results](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14273338&ad=5054350030&h=4PHWAhP&sig=TYD5JWtOcefjylCVOmypKyGENlT&v=2&isig=Pks7Qlv0KjQNzzITEyT6VKsW162&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/5pdvr2om/GPS-5498473-0/6582b0dd-9601-4959-a226-1f054ee5727a) as management guided 4Q gross margin ahead of expectations, indicated that 3Q represented peak near-term opex, & delivered double-digit ad revenue growth. [NFLX results were more mixed](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14273338&ad=5054350030&h=QqmfLCx&sig=N1fbYjU3fc3wpyH1o6NOiqjmojR&v=2&isig=Muy7cP2bqzZcb1qrpsiqzuCnals&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/-us7ltrd/GPS-5493996-0/6582b0dd-9601-4959-a226-1f054ee5727a), with UCAN Revenue growth accelerating, but the 2026 revenue outlook came down on an advertising shortfall and management deferred any specific 2027 commentary to the 4Q earnings call.

Note: SPCX is co-covered w/JPM’s Seth Seifman, Sebastiano Petti, & Richard
Choe.

Global Thematics & US Semiconductors  
Hot Summer, Short Fall: Increased Power Shortfall, Increased BTM Clarity, and
Addressing Rubin Rack kW Misconceptions  
| | [Read Full Report](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/0dfdfebc-cd73-11f1-98a3-da11e278520f?t=1792987434:7077:50140:527593380b83&m=1&ch=CDF Research ISG#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)  
---  
(PDF: 17 Pages)  
---  
| North America  
---  
Stephen C Byrd, Joseph Moore, David Arcaro, CFA, Cameron McVeigh, CFA, Sabrina
E Hao, Mason Wayne & 4 more...  
October 26, 2026  
---  
| | | ![](cid:image_0dfdfebc-cd73-11f1-98a3-da11e278520f_1_4)  
---  
Raising our 2026-28 net power shortfall (now including US DC spillover into
APAC) from 33GW to 38GW, driven by higher DC power demand, offset by greater
front-of-the-meter grid capacity (20GW from 15GW in '26-'28) & BTM. We address
key pushback, incl. power requirements for NVL72 Vera Rubin racks.  
---  
| | Key takeaways  
---  
  
  * Overall power demand from US DCs increases from 97GW to 116GW. Our power shortfall before time-to-power solutions increases from 57GW to 70GW. 
  * Both global and US power demand ests rise, reflecting (1) increased historical demand, (2) increased chip-level demand, and (3) utilized power assumptions. 
  * Power shortfall net of time-to-power solutions rises from 33GW to 38GW, after accounting for greater availability of BTM solutions & US DC spillover into APAC. 
  * We provide more color on areas of pushback: 1) BTM, 2) Asia spillover, 3) grid optimization/enhancing technologies, and 4) Vera Rubin configurations. 
  * We reiterate our conviction on 234kW/rack for Vera Rubin configurations, citing spec sheets and builds rather than derived values from chip spend. 

  
  
![](cid:image_0dfdfebc-cd73-11f1-98a3-da11e278520f_1_5)

We maintain convicted the power shortfall is real. We have received a
significant amount feedback on our power shortfall work as investors look to
square estimates for $1.5T / $1.6T of '27 / '28 capex with power availability
and what this means for the supply chain. We don't believe the idea of a ~33%
power shortfall is a consensus view, with many investors taking the stance
that companies will "creatively find ways around" these bottlenecks and citing
that orders in the supply chain remain strong. That being said, we still see
LPS as a key constraint to the buildout. Today, we update our Intelligence
Factory model to take into account new inputs — higher data center demand,
partially offset by higher front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter power
availability. This leads us to a 70GW '26-28 power shortfall _before_ time-to-
power-solutions (up from 57GW prior), or a 38GW '26-28 power shortfall _net_
of time-to-power-solutions and inclusive of US DC spillover into APAC (up from
33GW).

We also address key areas of investor pushback to our call, which is centered
around three levers of potential upside — 1) BTM, 2) Asia expansion, and 3)
grid enhancing technologies / data center curtailment — as well as our Vera
Rubin configuration assumptions. We'd note that while these three levers could
narrow the power shortfall further, they all face constraints of their own —
BTM deployment is constrained by labor and grid optimization/data center
curtailment can face stakeholder buy-in issues. On Asia, we forecast 15GW of
US demand spilling over into the region through 2030, and we now break this
out explicitly. On Vera Rubin configurations, we feel comfortable with our
assumptions, as they're in-line with NVDA and supply chain checks.

What does this mean for stocks? In our view, this shortfall will likely
increase the urgency, and premia paid, to secure (A) time-to-power solutions
in the US — for example, BTM players like BE and SEI, as well as the powered
shell providers (WULF,HUT,CIFR,RIOT). For a comprehensive list of ways to play
this theme, see (Exhibit 9 __) and (B) data center growth outside of the US —
read our Asia team's note on
this[here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/213a43b0-ad83-11f1-8ecd-723b2bfc0461).
For semis, we remain most constructive on NVDA and AVGO due to conservative
guidance, visibility into chip placement, geographic expansion outside the US,
and NVDA's higher token-per-watt profile. However, in event of a pause, we're
likely to see disruption at the tail of the bullwhip and where shortage driven
pricing dynamics are supporting revenue and EPS — such as downstream
components like memory,optical, and other components that are likely to be
over-ordered like power management and analog parts in a bear case (see more
here: [What Does the Power Shortfall Mean for
Semis](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/d204f72a-bb5d-11f1-b97f-fc33ff6c5a9f?ch=rp&sch=sr&sr=1)).
We see a risk that ASICs will lose share in a power-constrained environment
relative to GPUs, given the lower token production per watt for ASICs and
lower fungibility across customers.

Please see Exhibit 9— Ways to Play: Power Bottlenecks.

We have updated the Intelligence Factory model, our hub for Powering AI, the
power shortfall, token economics, and time-to-power solutions to reflect
increasing power demand. We now project 116GW of power demand from chips sold
in 2026-28, increased from 97GW. This increase comes from three changes to the
model:

  1. Increased expectations of _utility power_ necessary to power all purchased chips from increased demand of energy from storage, networking, and other rack-level components (previously excluded). 
  2. Increased _gross_ power demand from historical ex-Gen AI data centers.
  3. Proper squaring of an assumed 75% load factor within our power methodology, increasing overall power demand necessary to power chips at-capacity. 

Clearer methodology in defining/converting from _gross_ power (total, grid-
delivered power), _critical IT_ power (post-PUE power delivered to the chips),
and _utilized_ power (power that is "consumed" by the chips, inclusive of a
load factor) is necessary in evaluating the overall power demands of AI data
centers. Our updated model clearly outlines the designation of power (gross,
gross utilized, critical IT, etc.) within each line item and properly adjusts
between these designations to arrive at a total power demand. Further,
increased insight into [potential data center demand from our data centers
team](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/5e5cd1f8-c643-11f1-a2f0-77fc022c1a94)
(led by Cameron McVeigh; our projections of post-shortfall supply square
within a 3% margin of error in 2029, with lower margins in preceding years).

model.](mailto:Stephen.Byrd@morganstanley.com,Solomon.Thompson@morganstanley.com?subject=Requesting%20the%20Updated%20Intelligence%20Factory%20Model)

This increase in power comes as a result of fully factoring in the grid-level
power that must flow through to data centers in order to adequately power
chips through consistent inclusion of proper load factors. We reiterate that,
even with the presence of a shortfall, companies are incentivized to engage
with time-to-power solutions — our Intelligence Factory model projects
increasing margins on tokens produced in data centers while unit costs (both
per-token and production-per-watt metrics) fall with each subsequent chip
generation.

We see radically reduced cost/TFLOPs production across subsequent chip
generations as total costs v. unit costs fall in kind. These production
metrics are apparent in tokens produced/total wattage production, highlighting
the increases in token production efficiency and lending evidence to our
assertion that installing new-gen GPUs and Architectures justify the higher
up-front costs.

Key takeaways  
---  
  
  * We hosted MU COO, CTO, CFO, IR for investor meetings in NYC/Boston. Mgmt sees memory's strategic value in AI to remain high
  * Memory is the key enabler of AI perf, token/$, power efficiency. De-spec reflects memory shortages, not diminished value
  * Maintain Buy and a top pick on MU's leadership portfolio across HBM, DRAM, NAND with increased capital returns starting Dec-9

---|---|---  
  
* * *  
  
---  
  
Buy on mid/longer-term strategic value of memory

Following MU's Tech and Product webinar, we hosted COO Manish Bhatia, CTO
Scott DeBoer, CFO Mark Murphy, and IR CVP Satya Kumar for investor meetings in
New York and Boston. Overall, we are incrementally more positive on memory
after the meetings, with mgmt increasingly seeing CY27/28 to be tighter than
CY26. Key takeaways: 1) Memory remains the key enabler of AI perf and power
efficiency; 2) De-specs reflect shortages; more memory = higher token/$; 3)
SCAs greatly increase supply flexibility, spanning 3-5 years as take-or-pay
with financial commitments; 4) Tech leadership spans HBM, DRAM, NAND; 5)
Stronger capital returns begin on Dec-9. Maintain Buy and a top pick.

De-spec reflects memory constraints, not less significance

Memory is increasingly becoming the most critical architectural pillar in AI,
the key enabler of better perf, token/$, and power efficiency. Mgmt views
current memory de-spec as evidence of memory constraints, not other
constraints - compute, land, power and shell. Currently both GPU vendors and
hyperscalers have incentives to de-spec memory, given attractive compute
economics and relatively better availability of logic/CoWoS which they want to
fully monetize, even with less memory initially. Over time if memory becomes
available, system builders could re-spec memory again as it is the largest
contributor of token/$ and ROI (adding compute alone requires more power).

SCAs add flexibility in 3-5+ year supply, reduce volatility

Importantly, SCAs provide memory vendors much longer time to balance supply
together with their customers. Current SCAs span ~5 years, extending beyond
CY30 and with CY31 discussions already underway, vs. historical LTAs' limited
visibility of 1 year or less. As such, it has now become easier for memory
vendors to forecast bit demand growth 3-5 years out and have the flexibility
to reduce capex/tool spent in advance if demand slows. Moreover, all SCAs are
take-or-pay with committed bit volumes and financial commitments, with ~35% of
total sales expected to be covered under SCAs (~50% target by CY30) with
pricing framework whose price floor is well above prior cycle high.

Roadmap confidence across HBM, DRAM and NAND

MU flagged the ability to support HBM 4-hi through 16-hi, custom HBM, vHBM (a
potential scalable alternative to SRAM) and vEIM (for edge applications). MU
expects to have four more planar DRAM nodes after 1-gamma, with 1-delta's
volume ramp targeted for 2H27. Meanwhile, mgmt downplayed 4F² DRAM and
believes capacitor scaling matters more than the cell footprint itself, with
MU's access to advanced litho extending MU's scaling runway - no customers
have shown interest in 4F². In NAND, G11 targets 400+ layers and twice G9's
bits by CY27-end. Adoption of SLC and TSV-enabled NAND may eventually depend
on customer interest, and MU is developing both techs.

Capital-return message clear: increase returns from Dec-9

Mgmt reiterated its intent to increase repurchases using prior quarter FCF (we
est. ~$150-200bn/yr FCF in CY27-28), beginning Dec-9 CHIPS restriction
deadline. Currently ~$35bn is authorized, with further authorization remains
subject to board approval.

---|---|---  
  
* * *  
  
---  
  
3Q Preview: Expect AWS to drive upside to estimates

Reports 10/29; we est. rev/EBIT at $202.0bn/$26.4bn vs Street at
$202.2bn/$26.1bn. We est. AWS growth of 40% y/y above Street at 38%, and we
expect upside to our ests. (+$4bn q/q rev. growth) driven by new capacity, YTD
price increases, ramp of AI Lab contracts, and growing enterprise inference
demand. We expect stable AWS margins at 39% in 3Q as higher depr. is offset by
strong utilization, growing Trainium workloads, Bedrock growth, and fee
increases. The key risk is high expectations (possibly at 42%+), but results
should suggest strong ROI on capacity capex.

Resilient Online retail spend in 3Q, Agentic in focus

Muse traction will likely drive questions on Amazon's agentic strategy. We
expect meet/beat sales as BAC aggregated credit & debit card data indicated
Online spend decelerated 4ppts q/q to 9% y/y, which is 6ppts better than
Street ests. for N.A. Retail growth to decelerate 10ppts q/q to 6% y/y. Ad
growth should decelerate due to Prime Day timing (we est 15% y/y growth vs 26%
in 2Q) but expect reacceleration in 4Q.

4Q Outlook: Expect 4Q guidance to bracket Street

Adobe ests. Oct. Big Deal Days sales was up 8.5%, while Amazon is upping
holiday hiring by 20%. For 4Q, slowing QTD Online retail spend is a risk, but
we expect rev. guidance of $239bn-$246bn (midpoint $242.5bn, +20% q/q), vs.
Street at $244.6bn. We expect an op. profit range of $29.0bn-$34.0bn vs.
Street at $32.9bn. AWS acceleration could drive 4Q profit upside, but 4Q is
driven by N.A. retail, where higher gas prices could be a 4Q margin headwind.

AWS positioning improving; Maintain Buy

Further improvement should be apparent in 3Q results that show AWS
acceleration and growing Bedrock & Trainium adoption aiding margins. Re:Invent
is a catalyst ahead that may have updates on Trainium 4, Bedrock, and possible
LLM development. Risks are capex growth & higher capital needs, 4Q cost
pressures from higher gas prices, and soft 3Q ad revs. (on Prime Day comp)
that fuel agentic concerns. Amazon's forward 2027E P/E multiple has contracted
from 29x (2025 YE) to 23x despite strong YTD results, so addressing Cloud
capacity ROI and Agentic risks to retail ad revenues could be key for stock
performance post print.

**Thoughts on the market.**



Last week was a tough one in tech hardware and semis. Not only did the SOX end
the week down -3.2% - taking us down -14.6% MTD and -18.5% from early Oct
highs – but there was pain under the surface that struck at different types of
investors.



JPM Position Intel is the best place to start: on Friday John Schlegel
commented that hedge fund alpha has been painful – and my own conversations
suggest that Thursday and Friday brought the most pain (TMT Momentum pair
ended down almost 5% on Thursday); yet HF selling on our book has
counterintuitively been moderate. **D****eclines this past week suggest a
combination of systematic de-risking, some further HF selling, plus a pullback
in retail demand…rather than a large liquidation event**.



  * **_Big picture:_** HFs ended Thursday -3.3%MTD globally. _On alpha, this has been the worst stretch in years_ , with Eq L/S 20d alpha (-2.9%) the worst since Feb '21 and Multi-Strat alpha the worst since Aug '24. 60d crowding returns (-4.1%) are back to July '24 levels (an episode that actually got a bit worse before it rebounded) … yet **HF selling on our book has been only moderate** (HF net flows were only -0.9z, gross -0.6z), with **multi-strat de-grossing slowed sharply**. **Quants also kept adding gross** , and **Retail buying (though slowed) also continued** and ETFs were tech buyers. **The steadier selling came from CTAs** (whose US equity exposure has fallen every day since 10/13). Mag7 is at the 52nd and Hyperscalers are down to 27th %-tile (LT). CTAs have cut their Nasdaq exposure, but ETF and Retail buyers are still adding Tech and Semis. Selling is giving signs of exhaustion here, but the same risks we discussed two seeks ago (namely high long-term semis positioning) remains a risk – especially if buyers remain sidelined. 



In terms of feedback we’ve been getting, _investors on Thursday and Friday
mainly complained about forced selling (pointing on Friday to convicted names
like CRDO, CLS & WDC), a buyer’s strike and lack of P&L to play offence_,
understandable given the FUD suffusing the market (including frontier ARR and
capital worries, midterms & geopolitics) and desire to hold on to P&L.****
